method: After freezing the decision and canonical pair, reopened the adopted EER and current programme overview. Recomputed credits, checked Articles 11, 12 and 23, the elective annex and earlier course description, then reconsidered the current workbook evidence and finished record.
findings: Maastricht European Law School is an English full-time 180 EC LLB with a European and comparative focus and no compulsory specialisation. Article 10 gives six compulsory first-year components (four of 11 EC and two of 8 EC), eight compulsory second-year components (two of 11 EC, five of 6 EC and one of 8 EC), then 48 EC electives and the 12 EC Final Legal Challenge. The elective phase has a learning plan, Annex 5 law electives and approved alternatives, including legal internships up to 12 EC, other faculties, study abroad and supervised individual content up to 6 EC. Non-law study is capped at 24 EC, eligible language study at 6 EC within that cap, and introductory study at 6 EC. Annex 4a identifies the selective four-year Madrid dual degree, outside the standard comparison.

The first-year binding advice threshold is 40 EC, subject to the stated exceptions. Law electives at Maastricht require completion of the first-year phase and are for third-year students. Second-year Private Law requires Introduction to Private Law. Law of the European Union requires International and European Law. Philosophy of Private Law requires Introduction to Private Law and Foundations of Law. Legal Research and Conflict Prevention and Resolution require successful completion of both first-year skills modules. Final Legal Challenge registration uses SLC3001 or SLC3002 after passing the Legal Research Legal Challenge (SLC2003), with the final result recorded under SLC3000. Article 12 requires an individual academic paper, public defence and final portfolio in English. The paper may concern international or EU law, national law approached comparatively or from a European perspective, or a meta-legal topic. The prior official course description corroborates portfolio, paper and presentation assessment and explains peer feedback within individual research. The standard degree does not itself confer professional qualifications.

Article 10 establishes 48 EC of restricted choices rather than requiring eight unnamed courses. The legal challenge has a distinct registration gate, an individual paper, a public defence and a portfolio. UCR gateway case briefing supports a partial introductory skills alignment. Comparative private law includes simulated mediation and the criminal course includes oral advice, which strengthens both comparisons without creating a standalone legal skills route. Current offerings and course order support both complete plans.
